document.title: Motion for Leave to Answer and Answer of Northern Virginia Electric Cooperative, Inc. to the Answer et al. of PJM Interconnection, L.L.C. filed on 09/10/2026

pages.text:
UNITED STATES OF AMERICA 
BEFORE THE 
FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION 
 
 
) 
 
PJM Interconnection, L.L.C. 
) 
Docket No. ER26-3380-000 
 
) 
 
 
MOTION FOR LEAVE TO ANSWER AND ANSWER OF 
NORTHERN VIRGINIA ELECTRIC COOPERATIVE, INC. TO MOTION FOR LEAVE 
TO ANSWER AND ANSWER OF PJM INTERCONNECTION, L.L.C. 
 
Pursuant to Rules 212 and 213 of the Rules of Practice and Procedure of the Federal 
Energy Regulatory Commission (“FERC” or the “Commission”),1 Northern Virginia Electric 
Cooperative, Inc. (“NOVEC”) respectfully submits this motion for leave to answer and answer to 
PJM Interconnection, L.L.C.’s (“PJM”) motion for leave to answer and answer (“PJM Answer”)2 
to NOVEC’s August 21, 2026, protest (“NOVEC Protest”)3 of the July 31, 2026, filing by PJM 
to revise its Open Access Transmission Tariff (“Tariff”) and Reliability Assurance Agreement 
Among Load Serving Entities (“RAA”) to establish the Reliability Backstop Procurement 
(“RBP”).4  
For the reasons set forth herein and in the NOVEC Protest, the Commission should reject 
the RBP as unjust and unreasonable. If the Commission does not reject the RBP, it should 
require revisions on compliance to eliminate or substantially reduce the nearly $2 billion 
collateral requirement that the RBP Proposal would impose on NOVEC, or set the collateral 
requirement for settlement and hearing judge procedures as suggested by PJM.5  
 
1 18 C.F.R. §§ 385.212-213.  
2 PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., Motion for Leave to Answer and Answer, Docket No. ER26-3380-000 (Sep. 10, 
2026) (Accession No. 20260910-5296) (“PJM Answer”). 
3 Northern Virginia Electric Cooperative, Inc., Protest, Docket No. ER26-3380-000 (Aug. 21, 2026) (Accession No. 
20260821-5307) (“NOVEC Protest”).  
4 PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., Reliability Backstop Procurement, Docket No. ER26-3380-000 (July 31, 2026) 
(Accession No. 20260731-5214) (“RBP Proposal”). 
5 PJM Answer at 92-93.

2 
 
I. 
MOTION FOR LEAVE TO ANSWER 
 
NOVEC respectfully requests leave to submit this answer. The Commission regularly 
allows answers for good cause shown, such as when the answers help ensure a more accurate and 
complete record, clarify the issues, or provide useful and relevant information that will assist the 
Commission in its deliberative process.6 This answer will correct PJM’s mischaracterizations of 
the context of the RBP framework, the unjust and unreasonable character of the RBP proposal, 
and the need to substantially revise PJM’s proposed collateral requirements for the Load Serving 
Entities (“LSE”) RBP Buyers. In addition, this answer provides useful and relevant information 
that will assist the Commission in its deliberative process. To the extent that this answer does not 
address an issue raised in PJM’s answer, that should not be construed as agreement with PJM. 
II. 
ANSWER TO PJM’S ANSWER TO THE PROTESTS AND COMMENTS ON 
THE RBP PROPOSAL 
A. Mr. Coscia’s Supplemental Affidavit explains the many flaws in PJM’s proposed 
collateral requirement that cause that proposal to be disconnected from its stated 
purpose and fundamentally onerous and not just or reasonable. 
With this answer, NOVEC includes a supplemental affidavit from Mr. Coscia.7 Mr. 
Coscia approaches the PJM collateral requirement from a methodological perspective.8 He points 
out that the amount of collateral should be related to the risk that an LSE fails to pay an RBP 
Charge and PJM’s methodology does not secure against that loss because it is focused on the risk 
that a large load fails to materialize.9 Mr. Coscia challenges PJM’s use of a uniform Credit 
 
6 See, e.g., City Utils. of Springfield, Mo. v. Sw. Power Pool, Inc., 168 FERC ¶ 61,085, P 51 (2019) (“We accept [the] 
answers…because they have provided information that assisted us in our decision-making process.”), order on reh’g 
& clarification, 170 FERC ¶ 61,024 (2020); Morgan Stanley Capital Grp., Inc. v. N.Y. Indep. Sys. Operator, Inc., 93 
FERC ¶ 61,017, at 61,036 (2000) (accepting an answer as “helpful in the development of the record”). See also, 
Hawtree Creek Farm Solar, LLC, 179 FERC ¶ 61,048, P 21 (2022); California Ridge Wind Energy, LLC, 175 FERC 
¶ 61,110, P 25 (2021); Pleinmont Solar 1, LLC, 173 FERC ¶ 61,126, P 18 (2020). 
7 See Supplemental Coscia Affidavit included with the instant filing.  
8 Id. P 8.  
9 Id. PP 9-16.

3 
 
Rate.10 He then turns to a discussion of the opt-out and the undefined MW amount to be 
secured.11 The Commission should also eliminate the resulting subsidization of the PJM capacity 
market by NOVEC and a relatively small number of other LSEs that would be primarily 
responsible for providing financial security for the contracts that PJM would enter into with RBP 
Resources. Mr. Coscia reviews PJM’s explanation of the collateral overlap between the RBP 
Charge collateral and the Peak Market Activity under Attachment Q.12 He concludes his affidavit 
by addressing the need for a reduction mechanism for the collateral obligation, discussing the 
stakeholder process, and opining on the need for a comprehensive overhaul of the credit 
methodology in the hearing and settlement judge procedures.13 
B. The capacity shortfall experienced by PJM resulted from a combination of causes in 
addition to growth of large customer load. 
 
PJM recognized in its original filing that the capacity shortfall it is seeking to address is 
the result of many causes, stating that “it is well-documented and recognized that supply and 
demand in the PJM Region have converged, as a significant portion of PJM’s thermal generation 
fleet have retired while replacement resources are arriving at a slower pace than the 
unprecedented load growth” and “[t]ogether, these factors have strained the RPM Auction’s 
ability to procure sufficient capacity to meet the PJM Region Reliability Requirement in recent 
capacity auctions.”14 Despite the other causes, PJM in answering NOVEC now maintains that 
“[t]he entire PJM Region is facing a capacity shortfall because entities like NOVEC contracted 
to serve new large loads on an unprecedented scale at an extremely rapid pace—without 
 
10 Id. PP 17-25.  
11 Id. PP 26-37. 
12 Id. PP 38-45. 
13 Id. PP 46-61. 
14 RBP Proposal at 28.

4 
 
requiring any associated new capacity.”15 PJM’s new interpretation of the context in which it 
urges the Commission to consider its filing is premised on two incorrect presumptions. 
 
First, NOVEC does not have any control over which customers receive electric service. 
Nor does NOVEC have a say in which customers choose to site in NOVEC’s service territory. 
NOVEC has an obligation under state law to serve its load, and NOVEC follows state law.  
 
Second, unlike Regional Transmission Organizations (“RTO”) like the Midcontinent 
Independent System Operator, Inc. (“MISO”), where the capacity market is a backup mechanism 
and LSEs are primarily responsible for meeting their resource adequacy requirements through 
bilateral arrangements,16 in PJM the Reliability Pricing Model (“RPM”) is the primary 
mechanism for LSEs to procure capacity. The Base Residual Auction in the RPM may allow 
LSEs to bilaterally contract for their capacity needs,17 but PJM operates the RPM to “ensure that 
enough capacity is procured, at a reasonable cost, to maintain reliable grid operations” and the 
rules do not indicate a maximum amount that LSEs can receive from PJM’s relevant capacity 
auctions.18  
 
For most utilities, the primary option is to buy capacity in the RPM, and there is no 
requirement for an LSE to bring its own new capacity.19 There is no basis for PJM’s criticism 
 
15 PJM Answer at 89.  
16 See Midcontinent Indep. Sys. Operator, Inc., 170 FERC ¶ 61,215, P 13 (2020) (“In other words, unlike the 
centralized capacity constructs used in the Eastern RTOs/ISOs, MISO’s Auction is not—and has never been—the 
primary mechanism for its LSEs to procure capacity.”) (emphasis in original). 
17 PJM Business Practice Manual No. 18 at § 1.2.1 (“Under RPM, each LSE that serves load in a PJM Zone during 
the Delivery Year shall be responsible for paying a Locational Reliability Charge equal to their Daily Unforced 
Capacity Obligation in the Zone multiplied by the Final Zonal Capacity Price applicable to that Zone. LSEs may 
choose to hedge their Locational Reliability Charge obligations by directly offering and clearing resources in the 
Base Residual Auction and Incremental Auctions or by designating self-supplied resources (resources directly 
owned or resources contracted for through unit-specific bilateral purchases) as self-scheduled to cover their 
obligation in the Base Residual Auction.”) (emphasis added). 
18 PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 190 FERC ¶ 61,084, P 3 (2025). 
19 PJM is now seeking to impose such an obligation through the pending Interim Resource Adequacy Service 
(“IRAS”) filing in Docket No. ER26-3515. PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., Proposal to Establish Interim Resource 
Adequacy Service and a Large Load Registry, Docket No. ER26-3515-000 (Aug. 13, 2026) (Accession No. 
20260813-5118) (“IRAS Filing”).

5 
 
that NOVEC did not secure its own generation, because NOVEC expected to procure capacity 
through the RPM as intended by the PJM Tariff. That does not make the shortfall NOVEC’s 
fault, or even its responsibility, as PJM now asserts. 
 
By filing the RBP, PJM is conceding that its RPM did not function as intended because 
there is a shortfall. The Commission should consider the RBP Proposal in light of the true 
context, namely that there are multiple causes of the present shortfall, that NOVEC reasonably 
relied on the RPM to procure its capacity, and that NOVEC is being forced to finance the 
construction of generation that will provide benefit to the region, as well as post an excessive 
collateral obligation to do so. 
C. The Commission should exercise its authority under NRG to require PJM to adopt 
the voluntary RBP framework approved in the stakeholder process, or in the 
alternative, reject the RBP Proposal with guidance on filing a voluntary iteration. 
 
The Commission should exercise its authority under NRG to require PJM to revise its 
RBP framework to conform to the voluntary, subscription-based, stakeholder-approved model, 
as NOVEC argued in its protest.20 PJM’s arguments do not establish that a voluntary model 
would not work. PJM contends that “a voluntary, subscription-based framework would not 
procure sufficient new capacity to meet demand and, in fact, would be highly likely to fail to 
cover that shortfall.”21 By way of evidence, PJM asserts that a voluntary framework is the “status 
quo”22 and that under the status quo, LSEs have not entered into bilateral agreements.23 PJM’s 
observation that LSEs have not entered into bilateral agreements prior to the filing of the RBP is 
immaterial and irrelevant. As NOVEC explained above, the RPM does not depend on bilateral 
 
20 NOVEC Protest at 24-26. 
21 PJM Answer at 16.  
22 Id. at 14. 
23 Id. at 15.

6 
 
arrangements. The RPM is intended to set prices needed to attract adequate generation and 
should not have to rely on LSEs promising out-of-market payments to function. 
 
That does not mean that the paradigm might not be subject to change on a going-forward 
basis and, indeed it should be subject to change if it is not working as currently designed. But the 
possible need for change is not grounds to criticize or blame market participants for conducting 
business in accordance with the current paradigm.  
 
As NOVEC explained in its protest, the voluntary model would allow the load to 
participate in the RBP or be interruptible.24 PJM’s own IRAS filing in Docket No. ER26-3515 is 
premised on the same mechanism to incentivize LSEs and load to “Bring Your Own New 
Capacity” (“BYONC”).25 Under IRAS, if new large loads do not participate with BYONC, they 
are subject to curtailment if PJM would order it and, to avoid the risk of curtailment, the new 
large loads are expected to bring their own new generation resources. Thus, it is puzzling why 
PJM maintains that a voluntary RBP model would not work but maintains that its IRAS proposal 
is just and reasonable and effective. 
 
In addition, a voluntary RBP model is more likely to be effective because many 
customers have already agreed to bear their costs through the Ratepayer Protection Pledge. 
While NOVEC is not, contrary to PJM’s assertion,26 a signatory to the Ratepayer Protection 
Pledge, NOVEC is supportive of the data center industry’s efforts to hold retail customers 
 
24 NOVEC Protest at 25 (“In NOVEC’s view, that control was critical to the success of the RBP process, which 
should embody a bottom-up, rather than a top-down approach. The bottom-up process gives truly interested 
developers the option to subscribe to pay the RBP costs rather than accept an interruptible form of service which 
PJM has proposed in Docket No. ER26-3515 (the Interim Resource Adequacy Service or ‘IRAS’). Contrary to the 
PJM Board’s determination, the voluntary subscription framework would provide sufficient assurance that capacity 
equal to the identified near-term shortfall would actually be procured. Paired with IRAS, committed load is 
adequately incentivized to participate to avoid an interruptible service—their business models rely on reliable 
service.”). 
25 See IRAS Filing at 23. 
26 PJM Answer at 59.

7 
 
harmless by funding their own power and transmission needs. As PJM points out, many such 
entities have committed to “‘build, bring, or buy the new generation resources and electricity 
needed to satisfy their new energy demands, paying the full cost of those resources whether by 
building, or buying from, new or otherwise additive power plants.’”27 Participating in a voluntary 
RBP framework would be a natural choice to accomplish what these customers have already 
agreed to do. 
 
PJM manifests a double standard in its comparison of a voluntary framework to its 
preferred RBP alternative. PJM specifically criticizes NOVEC for recognizing that a voluntary 
RBP may not procure the entire shortfall,28 arguing that NOVEC’s perspective “would 
effectively contradict the fundamental core reliability goal of the RBP to acquire the capacity 
shortfall….”29 However, in its transmittal letter, PJM conceded that because “RBP Resources 
shall not be partially cleared…there exists the possibility that PJM may clear a set of resources 
with a cumulative RBP UCAP MW total that does not exactly match the Final RBP Target.”30 In 
other words, PJM may not procure the entire shortfall through its own process. NOVEC should 
also add that, because of the expedited time frame, it is possible that an insufficient number of 
resources may bid at the required price level.31 It is unclear to NOVEC why PJM is willing to 
 
27 Id. (quoting Ratepayer Protection Pledge, The White House (Mar. 4, 2026), 
https://www.whitehouse.gov/releases/2026/03/ ratepayer-protection-pledge/ [https://perma.cc/N8PH-K82T]).  
28 Without acknowledging NOVEC’s observation that the IRAS would mitigate the consequences of any failure to 
procure the entire MW target through the voluntary RBP. NOVEC Protest at 25-26.  
29 PJM Answer at 16-17.  
30 RBP Proposal at 79.  
31 NOVEC Protest at 5 (“PJM’s timeline raises additional concerns that adversely affect the market. The success of 
the RBP depends on generators offering in sufficient quantities and at competitive prices. With only three weeks to 
make informed decisions based on the final, effective version of the RBP, some participants may not be able to 
prepare offers in time to participate. Indeed, PJM has requested FERC approval by September 29 so it can begin the 
RBP auction on September 30, which means that participants are expected to make decisions with impacts that last 
the better part of two decades in a span of a few weeks and without knowing what the actual rules or approved state 
regulator allocations will be.”).

8 
 
bear the risk that its preferred RBP alternative does not cover the shortfall in capacity, but views 
any risk that the voluntary model does not procure the total shortfall as a fatal flaw.  
 
The imposition of a voluntary process would also eliminate the contradiction of PJM’s 
opt-out mechanism. As Mr. Coscia explains in his supplemental affidavit, PJM justifies its opt-
out provision as addressing a limited regulatory gap faced by non-public utilities whose rates are 
not regulated by the states.32 In its answer, PJM argues that those customers are at the risk of an 
“overbuy” if large loads fail to materialize in the absence of state regulation.33 But the result is 
that one Virginia cooperative, Old Dominion Electric Cooperative, could opt out but another, 
NOVEC, could not.34 NOVEC’s exposure is not reduced by being state regulated because its 
customers may still have to absorb the cost of an overbuy notwithstanding state regulation.35 Mr. 
Coscia opines that “the economic rationale for the opt-out would be stronger if eligibility tracked 
the overbuy risk PJM identifies rather than state rate-regulatory status standing alone.”36  
There are two ways to effectuate Mr. Coscia’s opinion and align risk with the opt-out and 
NOVEC would support either. The Commission could extend the opt-out to all non-public 
utilities in recognition of the presence of the overbuy risk. Or the Commission could require PJM 
to adopt the voluntary, subscription-based RBP framework which would give all utilities and 
their customers the ability to manage their own exposure. The voluntary RBP framework 
eliminates the need for an opt-out by allowing utilities and their customers to enter arrangements 
that can effectively manage any overbuy risk.  
 
32 Supplemental Coscia Affidavit at P 26.  
33 PJM Answer at 30.  
34 Supplemental Coscia Affidavit at PP 27-28.  
35 Id. P 29.  
36 Id. P 31.

9 
 
 
The Commission should “exercise its authority under NRG to implement the voluntary 
subscription model the stakeholders approved as part of the CIFP process.”37 The PJM 
stakeholders sent the PJM Board an unambiguous message by achieving a clear consensus on a 
single proposal from more than a dozen considered.38 PJM’s observation that some stakeholders 
have supported the filed iteration of the RBP does not detract from the consensus achieved by the 
stakeholders on the voluntary, subscription-based framework.39 PJM’s removal of the ability of 
LSEs to accept RBP obligations fundamentally undermined the RBP process, which was 
intended to embody a bottom-up,40 rather than top-down approach, and was one part of an 
interconnected series of proposals intended to comprehensively address PJM’s resource 
adequacy challenges.41 The Commission should honor the consensus achieved by the 
stakeholders rather than allow PJM to pick and choose proposals it likes without regard for the 
compromises that led to the whole package, a process that undermines trust in the stakeholder 
process.  
D. The Commission should reject PJM’s argument that NOVEC misrepresents the 
cost-allocation standard because the RBP filing violates the Commission’s cost-
causation principles. 
 
NOVEC explained in its protest that the RBP violates the Commission’s cost-causation 
principle because it would assign all costs to one cause of the capacity shortfall without 
 
37 NOVEC Protest at 24.  
38 Id. 24-25.  
39 PJM Answer at 13. 
40 As Mr. Coscia explains in his supplemental affidavit, the voluntary RBP MWs would be fully secured and would 
not expose ratepayers to additional risk above PJM’s proposal. Supplemental Coscia Affidavit at P 58. 
41 NOVEC Protest at 25; East Kentucky Power Cooperative, Inc., Protest, Docket No. ER26-3380-000, at 
Attachment 1 Affidavit of Adam Bednarcyzk at P 16 (Aug. 21, 2026) (Accession No. 20260821-5322) (“EKPC 
Protest”) (“By contrast, PJM's filed proposal largely treats procurement, cost allocation, and the forthcoming IRAS 
process as separate constructs. PJM states that the RBP does not depend on the IRAS framework. That separation 
breaks the direct connection between the entity creating the incremental reliability need and the consequences of 
failing to mitigate that need. Unlike the Coalition proposal, the filing does not establish a unified framework that 
carries responsibility from procurement through settlement and operational consequences. As a result, it does not 
provide the same transparent and traceable path for ensuring that large-load customers and their suppliers remain 
reliability neutral.”).

10 
 
recognizing the impact of other causes, such as generation retirement driven by state policy 
choices,42 and because it creates benefits for other capacity customers in PJM by forcing 
generation subsidized by NOVEC to bid into the capacity market as a price-taker.43 As NOVEC 
clarified, “PJM’s requirement that RBP Resources offer at $0 can affect the RPM clearing price, 
and any resulting price reduction benefits capacity purchasers beyond the LSEs required to bear 
the incremental costs of supporting those resources.”44 The reasoning behind the premise is 
simple. The cost-causation principle requires the Commission to have “an articulable and 
plausible reason” to believe that the benefits are roughly commensurate with the costs.45 
 
PJM argues that NOVEC “seeks to establish a false standard for cost allocation 
approaches.”46 PJM argues that “all approved rates reflect to some degree the costs actually 
caused by the customer who must pay them”47 and “[t]o the extent an entity causes the costs to 
be incurred, it will have to pay its share.”48 PJM stresses that the Commission is not required to 
ensure full or perfect cost causation,49 and argues that the RBP Proposal “easily meets this 
standard.”50 PJM argues that it meets this standard because it tracked the Load Adjustments to 
the zones/areas where they occurred and allocated the costs to the Electric Distributor zones and 
this was the most granular way available to PJM to allocate costs.51 
 
Granularity is beside the point. PJM cannot assert that NOVEC has articulated a false 
standard because PJM did not acknowledge or even engage with NOVEC’s arguments. PJM did 
 
42 NOVEC Protest at 9-14. 
43 Id. at 15-17.  
44 Id. at 17.  
45 Illinois Commerce Comm’n v. FERC, 576 F.3d 470, 477 (7th Cir. 2009). 
46 PJM Answer at 62.  
47 Id. (quoting KN Energy Inc. v. FERC, 968 F.2d 1295, 1300 (D.C. Cir. 1992) (internal citations omitted)). 
48 PJM Answer at 62.  
49 Id. (quoting S.C. Pub. Serv. Auth. v. FERC, 762 F.3d 41, 88 (D.C. Cir. 2014)).  
50 PJM Answer at 62. 
51 Id. at 62-63.

11 
 
not challenge NOVEC’s argument that there are other causes for the shortfall besides load 
growth or that other customers will benefit from NOVEC paying for generation to bid as a price-
taker in the RPM. NOVEC pointed out that thousands of MWs of retirements were caused by 
state policies and that a reduction in generation is a key cause of the shortfall.52 Bidding as price-
takers can cause lower RPM prices because those offers “crowd out other capacity that is priced 
at a higher, cost-based rate” and thereby produce a lower clearing price.53 PJM explained that to 
“the extent an entity causes the costs to be incurred, it will have to pay its share,” which is 
exactly how NOVEC described the cost-causation principle and why PJM’s proposed cost 
allocation violates that principle. 
 
The Commission “may never approve unjust and unreasonable rates by allocating costs to 
those who reap little to no benefit…nor may it choose not to allocate costs to ‘those who cause 
the costs to be incurred and reap the resulting benefits.’”54 In other words, the Commission 
cannot approve a cost-allocation scheme that ignores beneficiaries and other causes of the 
shortfall. If it does not reject the RBP Proposal as unjust and unreasonable, the Commission 
should modify PJM’s cost-allocation approach to reflect the benefits received by the rest of PJM 
by adjusting the RBP Charges to account for those benefits and reducing the RBP collateral 
requirement to reflect those same benefits. 
 
52 NOVEC Protest at 11.  
53 New Jersey Board of Public Utilities v. FERC, 744 F.3d 74, 85 (3d Cir. 2014). It goes without saying that in 
addition to the price depressive effect benefiting other customers, it also distorts the PJM capacity market signals by 
altering the price signals being sent. The Commission should not lose sight of the fact that a cost-based intervention 
is not going to solve the problems with PJM’s market structure. It becomes, as former Chairman Christie warned, 
another iteration of the “perpetual tweaking” needed to keep the RPM moving forward. NOVEC Protest at 13 
(quoting Mark C. Christie, It’s Time to Reconsider Single-Clearing Price Mechanisms in U.S. Energy Markets, 44 
Energy L.J. 1, 26 (2023)). Before the Commission approves another kludge for the RPM, it should consider, as 
discussed above, whether the voluntary option interfaces better with PJM’s market design. 
54 El Paso Elec. Co. v. FERC, 76 F.4th 352, 362 (5th Cir. 2023) (quoting Nat’l Ass’n of Reg. Util. Comm’rs, 475 
F.3d 1277, 1285 (D.C. Cir. 2007) (emphasis added)).

12 
 
E. The collateral requirement is unjust and unreasonable because it is duplicative, 
excessive, and the initial credit rate is insupportably high. The collateral 
requirement should be revised to allow other forms of collateral.  
a. The collateral requirement is subjective, unduly discriminatory, and unjust 
and unreasonable because it is excessive. 
 
PJM’s proposed collateral requirement is not just and reasonable. PJM asserts that its 
methodology strikes an appropriate balance between protecting PJM’s markets and ensuring 
market participants have adequate flexibility to manage their collateral requirements.55 PJM 
notes that the Commission has cautioned against overly conservative credit requirements that are 
poorly correlated to credit risk that would impose costs.56 PJM’s methodology does not strike 
that balance. 
 
As a threshold matter, not even PJM can reasonably claim that its proposal ensures 
market participants have adequate flexibility to manage their collateral requirements. Market 
participants have no flexibility to manage their collateral requirements. They must post the full 
amount, with no exceptions for individual credit risk and subject only to intermittent and 
irregular reductions at PJM’s discretion.57 PJM has set the obligation so high for NOVEC that 
neither option is practicable.58 As Mr. Coscia explained in his affidavit, “[c]ash is not available” 
because the obligation “is approximately eight times [NOVEC’s] entire cash and temporary 
investments and approximately 3.4 times all of its current and accrued assets.”59 A letter of 
credit, if one could be had, “would have to be supported by [NOVEC’s] balance sheet.”60 The 
 
55 PJM Answer at 84. 
56 Id. (quoting PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 186 FERC ¶ 61,055, P 28 (2024)).  
57 RBP Proposal, Attachment A at § 18.8(b)(i)(A) (“...the RBP Credit Rate shall equal $1.5 million, as may be 
reduced, for reasons including a change in the total committed RBP UCAP MW, when total posted RBP Collateral 
is greater than the total remaining RBP Charges obligations, over time by the Office of the Interconnection to an 
amount sufficient to cover the total existing RBP Charges obligations….”) (italics added). 
58 NOVEC Protest, Rollins Affidavit at 3:7-16.  
59 NOVEC Protest, Coscia Affidavit at P 64 (“NOVEC Coscia Affidavit”). 
60 Id. P 65.

13 
 
Rural Utilities Service holds a mortgage over most of NOVEC’s assets and its loan documents 
limit the incurrence of additional secured obligations and liens.61 The carrying cost would 
consume NOVEC’s entire operating margin even under the most favorable circumstances, but, 
realistically, the cost is likely to be multiples of the margin, forcing NOVEC into a permanent 
net-loss position for the foreseeable future due to following the rules set out before it and then 
having those rules drastically changed without any consideration.62 
 
PJM cannot reasonably claim that the collateral requirement is necessary to protect PJM’s 
markets because it has, at best, a limited correlation to the risk to PJM’s markets.63 Mr. Coscia 
explained that the RBP settles as a contract for differences and NOVEC pays the difference 
between the RBP price and the RPM clearing price for the year, multiplied by its allocated RBP 
UCAP MW.64 NOVEC does not pay the RBP price and when the RPM clears above it, NOVEC 
receives a payment.65 As Mr. Coscia explains, PJM has not linked the collateral obligation to the 
risk of loss because it is based on the RBP Resources’ revenue and not what would remain 
payable on default.66 The credit rate is theoretical, dismissive of likely outcomes and 
disconnected from NOVEC’s obligation: 
Because the Credit Rate makes no reference to RPM, the requirement bears 
no stable relationship to what the cooperative will owe. Where RPM clears 
close to the RBP price the difference approaches zero while the collateral 
does not move. Where RPM clears far below it the difference widens and 
 
61 Id. 
62 Id. P 66 (“Carrying cost compounds the problem. Taking the most favourable assumption available — that a letter 
of credit can be obtained at 100 basis points — the annual cost would be approximately $19.5 million. The 
cooperative reported patronage capital and operating margins of approximately $20.8 million for 2025, after existing 
interest expense of approximately $0.8 million. At 100 basis points the carrying cost alone would consume 
approximately 94 percent of that margin; at 150 basis points, approximately 141 percent; at 200 basis points, 
approximately 188 percent; and at 300 basis points, approximately 281 percent. Each is between approximately 
twenty-five and seventy-five times the cooperative's entire existing annual interest expense, and each would recur 
for as long as the requirement remains outstanding.”).  
63 See Supplemental Coscia Affidavit at P 12 (“Gross contractual value therefore is not itself a measure of loss on 
default.”) 
64 NOVEC Coscia Affidavit at P 38; see also RBP Proposal at 59-60.  
65 See NOVEC Coscia Affidavit at P 38.  
66 Supplemental Coscia Affidavit at PP 9-12.

14 
 
the collateral is unchanged again. A requirement calibrated to exposure 
would vary with the second price; this one is fixed against the first.67 
 
Mr. Coscia points out that a collateral requirement is ordinarily derived from three components: 
an identified position, a price at which the position would be replaced, and a period of time of 
exposure.68 The size of the residual loss should be identified before the amount of collateral to 
absorb it is decided and “a formula based on approximately one-half of gross contractual value 
does not establish that relationship.”69 Mr. Coscia attempted to estimate total exposure based on 
RPM clearing prices over 13 years and the full 15 years based on a conservative assumption that 
the RBP would clear at $555/MW-day.70  
 
It is worth noting that PJM clarified that no collateral requirement would be required for 
years that RBP Resources are not in service.71 Mr. Coscia calculated an exposure at $200 to $290 
million for two years without RBP Resources receiving the RPM clearing price because they 
were not in service.72 NOVEC will not have charges for that period, which means that his 
estimate for the 13-year exposure is closer to reality. Even using his lifetime exposure of 15 
years, the total collateral obligation never dropped below the total exposure and was as high as 
ninefold.73 As a multiple of the 13-year exposure (the true lifetime exposure), the collateral 
obligation now ranges, depending on the RPM clearing prices, from multiples of 1.1 to 1,149. 
Although Mr. Coscia does not forecast the RPM clearing prices, he does opine that if the RBP 
“does not resolve the shortfall and the Interim Resource Adequacy Service is not implemented,

prices would in my opinion almost certainly clear above the present cap once the collar comes

Mr. Coscia comments that the table shows “that the filed requirement exceeds the 
exposure at every path in the range.”75 PJM did not in its answer to NOVEC’s protest address the 
substance of the affidavit Mr. Coscia submitted on behalf of NOVEC, perhaps because it 
confirms that PJM’s collateral obligation is excessive. Requiring NOVEC to post collateral that 
protects the PJM market potentially multiples above its total exposure is excessive and does not 
satisfy the Commission’s requirement that the collateral obligation strike an appropriate balance 
between protecting the market and facilitating market participation. “Magnitude is the measure 
of” limiting access to the market.76 NOVEC’s nearly $2 billion collateral requirement is close to

Participants.77  
 
Further, NOVEC demonstrated that the collateral obligation contemplated by the RBP 
was partly duplicative of the collateral amounts already held by PJM.78 PJM argues that the RBP 
collateral is not duplicative of the Peak Market Activity collateral PJM requires for transactions

provider of last resort for that load becomes responsible on a going-forward basis.”80 In contrast, 
PJM “envisions that an LSE’s obligation to pay RBP Charges should not be shunted to a 
provider of last resort—the idea is that the large load driving the need for the RBP should bear

the Delivery Year and every “LSE carries, as a matter of course, a forward RPM capacity 
obligation extending roughly three years.”82    
 
Notwithstanding PJM’s unclear argument premised on retail choice,83 the RBP Proposal 
indeed requires NOVEC to provide duplicative collateral.84 NOVEC provides PJM with a 
collateral amount that guarantees NOVEC will pay the recurring capacity costs every day. When 
NOVEC’s load grows by the Load Adjustment, it will likely provide additional collateral to 
account for the new capacity purchased above the original amount. At the same time, NOVEC 
would also be required to provide a collateral amount to PJM to guarantee its payment of the 
RBP Charge. The RBP Charge is a contract for difference.85 NOVEC will pay (or receive) the 
difference between the RBP Charge and the capacity clearing price. But PJM determines

price and the capacity clearing price. The capacity obligation has a three-year forward-looking 
time horizon which is, functionally, renewed each year for a successive three-year period for 
existing load. In effect, PJM is seeking to require NOVEC to post collateral for the same MWs 
of capacity twice. In particular, Mr. Coscia demonstrates that in the final three-year period, “an 
ordinary LSE and an RBP buyer carry forward RPM obligations of the same horizon at 
essentially the same price.”86 Coupled with the magnitude of the $2 billion requirement, the 
duplicative nature of the collateral obligation makes it excessive, and so the Commission should 
find that the RBP Proposal is not just and reasonable and reject it.87  
b. The Commission should require PJM to allow other methods of posting 
collateral. 
 
PJM argues that the collateral obligation should only be secured with cash or a letter of 
credit because “there is a likelihood that even entities with investment grade credit may see their

Charges that NOVEC could be responsible for represent, in any given year, a tiny fraction of the

for credit ratings to change, the greatest threat to NOVEC’s credit rating is PJM’s own RBP

Coscia pointed out that PJM “bills [NOVEC] weekly, observes whether it pays, and has an

in PJM.93  
 
PJM’s refusal to allow an unsecured credit allowance is inconsistent with every other 
credit policy it maintains. With respect to PJM’s existing credit policy, “[t]he general credit 
requirement is sized to Peak Market Activity, computed from a participant’s own observed 
billing history; unsecured credit allowances are keyed to creditworthiness and tangible net worth; 
and requirements are recalculated on an ongoing basis.”94 PJM’s only explanation for why it is 
refusing to allow an unsecured credit allowance is that in PJM’s experience, “Market Participants

during hot and cold-weather events.95 As Mr. Coscia cogently explains, “[c]redit migration over 
a fifteen-year horizon is a legitimate credit consideration” but “it does not explain why 
[NOVEC’s] credit condition should be ignored.”96 In contrast with the buyers, PJM’s seller

F. The RBP Proposal is unjust and unreasonable because it does not address 
underlying practical implementation issues and imposes unrealistic requirements. 
 
PJM relies in substantial part on the availability of mitigation to the RBP Charges and 
collateral obligation but gives only a limited window to make those arrangements. NOVEC 
would have to procure 1,619.2 MW to offset its obligation in the RBP auction.99 As a practical 
matter, NOVEC would not be able to prudently enter into the necessary transactions to procure 
such a large amount of power. The procurement process would require multiple counterparties 
and transactions, credit diligence, commercial and risk analyses, contract negotiations, internal 
approvals, and potential regulatory review, which could take from four to twelve months to 
negotiate.100 PJM has given NOVEC—and every RBP Buyer—ninety days. 
 
The expedited process rests on the viability of unproven assumptions. The obligation is 
fixed for 15 years even if the underlying load is delayed, reduced, canceled, or never 
materializes. For instance, PJM is relying on NOVEC’s 2025 aggregate LSE-level forecast even

profit cooperative and a transmission-dependent distribution utility, NOVEC faces a procurement challenge that is 
unusual both in magnitude and structure. A prudent procurement of more than 1,600 MW cannot reasonably be 
completed within the period PJM proposes. A procurement of this magnitude would likely require multiple 
counterparties and transactions, each involving counterparty and credit diligence, commercial and risk analysis,

though NOVEC’s 2026 forecast is lower. Or, for another example, PJM proposes to permit 
forecast-based RBP MW offsets for committed demand-side participation but does not explain 
how those commitments are reconciled with actual load.101 If the load does not materialize, it 
does not exist to be curtailed. 
 
Even if it were feasible to secure the RBP MW offsets, the procedures for an RBP Buyer 
to offset are not just and reasonable. Even though the Initial RBP Target is only 6,831.3 MW, 
PJM would require buyers to procure over 9,000 MW to eliminate their RBP allocations.102 
NOVEC would have to procure over 300 MW above its RBP allocation to remove its RBP 
allocation.103 The excess MW provide additional value to the PJM capacity market for which the 
RBP Buyer is not compensated. Further, any reductions NOVEC achieves are in effect shared 
with other RBP Buyers and vice versa, which, in addition to being unfair, creates a perverse 
incentive to free ride on others’ efforts.104 These provisions also mean that NOVEC will not 
know what its individual obligation is until the auction’s conclusion, which can create a material 
economic impact for a participant with as much exposure as NOVEC has.105 
 
PJM also asserts that NOVEC could use its existing collateral obligations with its 
customers to secure this new obligation or issue “low-interest, ratepayer-backed bonds” to meet 
the requirement.106 True or not, it is immaterial to the question of whether the collateral 
requirements asked by PJM are just and reasonable. To the extent that NOVEC can, NOVEC 
will explore every commercially reasonable option available to it if the collateral obligation is

imposed as PJM has requested. NOVEC requires a just and reasonable collateral obligation 
based on a just and reasonable methodology, which the RBP Proposal does not have. 
G. If the Commission does not reject the RBP Proposal, the Commission should 
require PJM to revise the PJM Tariff to precisely reflect commitments made in the 
PJM Answer. 
 
In its answer, PJM clarified that collateral for a Delivery Year will be based only on RBP 
UCAP MW committed for that year and that “no collateral would be required for RBP Resources 
[that] are not in service for that Delivery Year, and no RBP Charges would be assessed.”107 
NOVEC supports this clarification. However, NOVEC has reviewed Section 18.8(b)(i)(A), and 
PJM’s interpretation relies on the meaning of the term “committed” as it pertains to that section. 
PJM should be required to revise the proposed Tariff section to explicitly state that NOVEC and 
other LSEs with RBP obligations will not be required to post collateral for RBP Resources that 
are not in service. Mr. Coscia points out that Section 18.6(e) permits a resource to remain 
committed for up to three Delivery Years and Section 18.8(b)(i)(A) does not have an “in-
service” limitation, creating the risk that NOVEC could post collateral for an RBP Resource that 
does not operate during those three Delivery Years without clarification.108 
 
PJM also stated in its answer that the total collateral obligation “can decline as the 
remaining exposure declines.”109 The Commission should not approve the RBP Proposal with a 
provision that grants PJM the discretion not to reduce a collateral requirement that NOVEC has 
shown is already excessive. “A reduction that occurs only after remaining gross payments fall 
below posted collateral can leave the requirement unchanged for years despite changes in market 
prices, remaining tenor, or credit condition.”110 Given the enormous sums involved, the Tariff

should incorporate a mechanism to automatically reduce the collateral obligation with “objective, 
tariff-based standards…[that] state the frequency of review, the inputs used, the circumstances 
requiring a reduction, and the time within which excess collateral is returned.”111 
H. While PJM has not proposed a just and reasonable collateral framework for the 
RBP, if the Commission does not reject the RBP Proposal, the Commission should 
follow PJM’s suggestion to set the matter for further proceedings to decide the 
collateral obligation.  
 
To be clear, NOVEC believes that the RBP Proposal is not just and reasonable and 
should be rejected. However, to the extent that the Commission is inclined to approve the RBP 
Proposal, NOVEC would support the Commission “resolving the applicable buyer-side LSE 
RBP Credit Rate through additional procedures” as PJM suggests.112 
 
PJM indicates that it consents to keying the credit rate “to the actual MW-weighted 
average of the levelized procurement cost of all selected RBP Sell Offers that results from the 
RBP and not the maximum of such value” and references the NOVEC Protest for clarity on the 
description.113 “Using the actual RBP procurement price would reduce the requirement if the 
procurement clears below $555/MW-day” but “[i]t would not resolve the underlying 
methodology.”114 NOVEC supports this minor modification to the credit requirement, but would 
stress to the Commission that, in order to be most conducive to settlement, the scope of the 
hearing and settlement judge procedures set on the RBP Buyer-side credit requirement should 
encompass the entire collateral framework.115

III. 
CONCLUSION 
WHEREFORE, for the foregoing reasons, NOVEC respectfully requests that the 
Commission grant this motion for leave to answer, accept NOVEC’s answer, and reject the RBP 
Proposal. In the alternative, NOVEC respectfully requests that the Commission order PJM to 
modify the RBP as requested herein to eliminate or substantially reduce the collateral obligation 
and set the entire RBP buyer-side credit requirement for hearing and settlement judge 
procedures.
